title: What a Car Is Made Of
subtitle: Engine, transmission, chassis, suspension, brakes — the parts a mechanic will name, and what each one does.
description: A B1 technology reading and listening text explaining the main systems of a car in plain English, with vocabulary and comprehension exercises.
passage: A car has thousands of parts, but almost all of them belong to one of about six systems. If you know what those six do, you can follow most of what a mechanic tells you, and you can describe a problem in a way that gets it fixed.

The engine produces the power. In a petrol or diesel engine, fuel burns inside sealed cylinders, and the force of each small explosion pushes a piston down. The pistons turn a crankshaft, which converts that up-and-down movement into the rotation the car actually needs, and valves open and close to let fuel and air in and exhaust gases out. Timing is everything: the valves, the pistons and the ignition have to act within thousandths of a second of each other. An electric car does away with all of it. A battery supplies current to one or more motors, and the motors turn directly — far fewer moving parts, and almost no noise.

The transmission decides how that power reaches the wheels. An engine only produces useful power across a narrow range of speeds, so the transmission uses gears to keep it inside that range whether the car is pulling away from a stop or travelling at a hundred kilometres an hour. A low gear gives more turning force and less speed, which is what you want on a hill; a high gear gives the opposite. A manual transmission makes the driver choose; an automatic chooses for them. Electric motors produce their full turning force from a standstill, which is why most electric cars need only a single gear.

From the transmission, the power passes through the drivetrain — the shafts and the differential — to the wheels. The differential exists because of a problem that is easy to miss: when a car turns a corner, the outside wheel travels further than the inside one, so the two cannot be locked together at the same speed. The differential lets them turn at different rates. Cars send this power to the front wheels, the rear wheels, or all four, and all-wheel drive gives more grip on a loose or wet surface.

The chassis is the structure everything else is attached to — usually steel, sometimes aluminium, and designed as much to absorb the energy of a crash as to hold the car together. Mounted on it is the suspension: springs, dampers and the arms that hold the wheels in position. Its job is not only comfort. A wheel that bounces off the road surface is a wheel that is not steering or braking, so suspension is a safety system as much as a ride-quality one.

The wheels and tyres are the only parts of a car that touch the road, and every force — accelerating, braking, cornering — passes through four contact patches each about the size of a hand. Tyre condition therefore matters more than most drivers assume. Inside the wheels are the brakes: a disc that turns with the wheel, and a caliper that squeezes pads against it. The friction converts the car's movement into heat, which is why brakes get extremely hot and why they fade when used hard for too long.

Finally there is the cabin and its controls. The steering system turns the wheel's rotation into movement at the front wheels through a rack and pinion. The dashboard reports what the car is doing. Modern cars add a great deal more — screens, climate control, cameras, sensors that brake for you if you do not — but the underlying six systems are unchanged. The car still burns or stores energy, converts it to rotation, sends it to the wheels, holds itself together, stays in contact with the road, and stops.

exercises.title: Understanding the Text
exercises.instructions: Each of these asks why a part exists, not only what it is called.

options: It converts the pistons' up-and-down movement into rotation
It controls when the valves open
It supplies fuel to the cylinders
items.explanation: The engine produces linear movement; the wheels need rotation. The crankshaft is what bridges them.

items.prompt: Why does a car need a transmission at all?
options: To reduce the noise the engine makes
Because an engine only produces useful power across a narrow range of speeds
To reverse the direction of the crankshaft
items.explanation: The gears keep the engine inside that range “whether the car is pulling away from a stop or travelling at a hundred kilometres an hour”.

items.prompt: Why do most electric cars need only one gear?
options: Because they are driven more slowly
Because their motors produce full turning force from a standstill
items.explanation: The problem gears exist to solve does not arise in the same way.

options: Because in a corner the outside wheel travels further than the inside one
Because the front and rear axles rotate in opposite directions
Because the engine turns faster than the wheels
items.explanation: The text calls it “a problem that is easy to miss” — the two wheels cannot be locked at the same speed through a turn.

items.prompt: Why does the writer say the suspension is a safety system?
options: Because it protects the passengers in a crash
Because it stops the chassis from bending
Because a wheel bouncing off the road is not steering or braking
items.explanation: “Its job is not only comfort” — keeping the tyre in contact with the road is what keeps the driver in control.

items.prompt: Why does the text say tyre condition matters more than drivers assume?
options: Because tyres are expensive to replace
Because every force passes through four contact patches about the size of a hand
items.explanation: Accelerating, braking and cornering all act through that very small total area.

options: The friction converts movement into heat, and they overheat when used hard for too long
The caliper loses pressure at speed
items.explanation: “Which is why brakes get extremely hot and why they fade when used hard for too long.”

items.prompt: What is the writer's point in the final sentence?
options: That modern electronics have replaced the mechanical systems
That the six basic jobs a car does are unchanged, however much technology is added
That older cars were simpler to repair
items.explanation: The list at the end restates the six systems as six jobs — the frame the whole text was built on.

exercises.title: True or False?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether each statement matches the text.

items.statement: A low gear gives more turning force and less speed.
items.explanation: True — “which is what you want on a hill”. A high gear does the opposite.

items.statement: Electric cars have more moving parts than petrol engines.
items.explanation: False — “far fewer moving parts, and almost no noise”.

items.statement: All-wheel drive improves grip on a loose or wet surface.
items.explanation: True — given as the reason for sending power to all four wheels.

items.statement: The chassis is designed only to hold the car together.
items.explanation: False — it is designed “as much to absorb the energy of a crash” as to hold the car together.

items.statement: Brakes work by converting movement into heat.
items.explanation: True — through friction between the pads and the disc.

items.statement: A manual transmission chooses the gear for the driver.
items.explanation: False — that is an automatic. A manual “makes the driver choose”.

exercises.title: Part and Purpose
exercises.instructions: Match each part to the job it does.

pairs.right: pushed down inside the cylinder by burning fuel
keeps the engine in its useful speed range
lets the driven wheels turn at different speeds in a corner
keeps the tyres in contact with the road
squeezes the pads against the brake disc
turns steering-wheel rotation into side-to-side movement

items.explanation: In order, these trace the path energy takes through a car: from the explosion in the cylinder all the way to the road, and then back to a stop.

exercises.title: Talking to a Mechanic
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with the right term.

items.prompt: There is a noise from the ___ when I go over bumps.
items.explanation: The suspension is what deals with bumps, so that is where a bump-related noise comes from.

items.prompt: The brakes started to ___ on the long descent.
items.explanation: To fade is to lose effectiveness through overheating — exactly what a long descent causes.

items.prompt: The tyres have almost no ___ left in the wet.
items.explanation: Grip is the hold a tyre keeps on the road surface.

items.prompt: The ___ is slipping — it will not stay in third ___.
items.explanation: The transmission holds the gears; slipping out of gear is a transmission fault.

items.prompt: The car will not start — I think it is the ___.
items.explanation: The ignition sets the fuel alight; if it fails, the engine will not run at all.

items.prompt: The ___ between the pads and the disc turns movement into heat.
items.explanation: Friction is the resistance between two surfaces rubbing together.

discussion: The text says knowing the six systems lets you describe a problem so it gets fixed. Have you ever struggled to explain a fault to a specialist?
Electric cars remove most of the moving parts. What is gained, and is anything lost?
Which of the six systems would you least want to fail while driving, and why?
Do you think drivers should have to understand how a car works, or is that the mechanic's job?
Write about 120 words explaining how something you use every day works, naming its parts and what each one does.
